lesson.title: The Number That Makes AC Behave Like DC: RMS Value
lesson.summary: RMS value is the equivalent steady DC value that would deliver the same average power as an AC waveform, and for a sine wave it sits at a fixed, calculable fraction of the peak value.
lesson.body:
An AC voltage is constantly changing, sweeping from zero up to its peak, back through zero, down to its negative peak, and back again, so quoting a single voltage number for an AC signal is not as simple as it is for a steady DC battery. Two natural candidates come to mind first: the peak value, the single highest point the waveform reaches, and the average value, the mean of the waveform over some interval. Both are useful, but neither answers the question that matters most for power delivery: how much heat would this AC signal produce in a resistor, compared to a steady DC voltage? RMS, short for root mean square, answers exactly that question, and it is defined so that an RMS voltage of V produces the same average power in a resistor as a DC voltage of the same value V.

For a pure sine wave, RMS has a fixed, derivable relationship to the peak value: Vrms = Vm divided by the square root of 2, approximately 0.707 Vm, where Vm is the peak value. This factor comes directly from averaging the square of a sine wave over one full cycle, since sin squared of omega t averages to exactly 0.5 over a complete cycle, and taking the square root of that 0.5 gives 1 over the square root of 2. Note that RMS is not the same as the average value: the plain average of a full sine cycle is zero, since the positive and negative halves cancel exactly, which is why average value is normally quoted over just a half cycle instead, where it works out to Vavg = 2 Vm divided by pi, approximately 0.637 Vm.

Worked example: North American wall outlets are rated at 120 volts, and that rating is an RMS value, not a peak value. Using Vrms = Vm over the square root of 2, the actual peak voltage on the wire is Vm = Vrms times the square root of 2 = 120 times 1.41421, approximately 169.7 volts, commonly rounded to about 170 volts. Checking this in reverse confirms the relationship: Vrms = 170 divided by 1.41421, approximately 120.2 volts, matching the nominal 120 V rating closely. The half cycle average value of that same waveform would be Vavg = 2 times 170 divided by pi = 340 divided by 3.14159, approximately 108.2 volts, a third distinct number from both the 170 V peak and the 120 V RMS, illustrating why it matters which of the three is being quoted.

The reason RMS earns its central role in AC power calculations is that formulas like P = V squared over R and P = I squared times R work correctly with AC signals only when V and I are RMS values, without needing any extra correction factor. This is exactly why every AC voltmeter, every appliance nameplate, and every utility bill is expressed in RMS volts and RMS amps by default, even though the instantaneous voltage is constantly swinging far above and below that number. A 120 V RMS supply genuinely delivers the same heating power to a resistor as a steady 120 V battery would, even though the AC voltage briefly reaches nearly 170 volts on every cycle.

It is worth remembering that the Vm over root 2 relationship applies specifically to pure sine waves. Other waveform shapes, square waves, triangle waves, or the pulsed output of some power supplies, have different RMS to peak ratios entirely, so the 0.707 factor should never be assumed automatically without confirming the waveform is genuinely sinusoidal.
